title: Я, ю, є, ї, й, the soft sign and the apostrophe
objectives: I can read the six new letters 'й', 'я', 'ю', 'є', 'ї' and 'ь', say their names, and find any of the 33 letters in the alphabet.
I can explain the two jobs of 'я', 'ю' and 'є', a [j] sound plus a vowel or a vowel that softens the consonant before it, and why 'ї' is always [ji].
I can tell hard from soft consonants and explain what the soft sign does in words such as 'день' and 'сіль'.
I can explain why the apostrophe is written in 'ім’я́' and 'м’я́со', and read a doubled consonant such as the 'тт' of 'життя́' as one long sound.
I can read any Ukrainian word aloud from its spelling by following a fixed procedure.

vocabulary.note: [t͡ʃɑj]: the 'й' at the end is [j], the 'y' of 'yes', so the word rhymes with English 'my'. One syllable, so it has no stress mark.

The letter 'я' is also this whole word, [jɑ]. Inside a sentence it is written with a small letter, unlike English 'I': 'Тара́с і я', Taras and I. Ukrainian uses no word for 'am', so 'Я Андрі́й.' is literally 'I Andrii'.
[iˈmjɑ]: the apostrophe keeps the 'м' hard and the [j] of 'я' sounded. Said of a person, it is the first name, not the family name.
[sʲiˈmjɑ]: the 'с' is soft before 'і', then the apostrophe keeps the 'м' hard and gives [jɑ]. It names the household: parents and their children.
[ˈmjɑsɔ]: a hard [m], then [j], then [ɑ]. The apostrophe shows this order of sounds.

example.source: This is meat, and this is fish.

vocabulary.note: [zɛmˈlʲɑ]: the 'я' after 'л' makes the 'л' soft and gives a plain [ɑ], with no [j]. Written with a capital, 'Земля́' is the planet Earth.

example.source: The house is here, and the land is there.

vocabulary.note: The 'н' is soft before 'я', and the 'с' just before it is said soft as well. The 'я' after a consonant has no [j].
[klʲut͡ʃ]: the 'ю' after 'л' makes the 'л' soft and gives a plain [u]. It is the key to a door or a lock.

[jɛ]. It is the present form of the verb 'бу́ти', to be, and it never changes its form. It says that something exists or is present. Most sentences that say what or where something is have no verb at all, as in 'Чай тут.', so 'є' is not the word for 'is'. A later unit explains its uses.
[ˈjɑblukɔ]: 'я' at the start of a word is [jɑ], the 'ya' of 'yard'.
[ukrɑˈjinɑ]: the 'ї' after the vowel 'а' is [ji], and it carries the stress. Four syllables: У-кра-ї-на.
[ˈkɪjiw]: the 'ї' is [ji], and the final 'в' is [w], as in 'cow'. Other forms use the stem 'Ки́єв-', where 'є' after the vowel 'и' is [jɛ].
[ˈjiʒɑ]: 'ї' at the start of a word is [ji], the 'yea' of 'yeast'. It means food in general.
[lʲʋiw]: the soft sign makes the 'л' soft with no vowel after it. The first 'в' is [ʋ] before 'і', and the last is [w]. One syllable, so it has no stress mark. Other forms use the stem 'Львов-'.
[sʲilʲ]: the 'с' is soft before 'і', and the 'л' is soft before the soft sign. Compare 'стіл', table, which ends in a hard 'л'.

example.source: The salt is here, and the sugar is there.

vocabulary.note: [dɛnʲ]: the 'д' is hard before 'е', and the 'н' is soft before the soft sign.

example.source: Here it is day, and there it is evening.

vocabulary.note: [ˈɔsʲinʲ]: the 'с' is soft before 'і', and the 'н' is soft before the soft sign.

example.source: Here it is autumn, and there it is winter.

vocabulary.note: [ʒɪˈtʲːɑ]: the doubled 'тт' is one long consonant, soft because 'я' follows. Hold the [tʲ] instead of saying it twice.
It begins with a soft [sʲ] followed by [ɔ], written 'сьо'. The 'н' is soft before 'і', and the 'д' before it is said soft as well.

grammar.title: The full alphabet: 'й' and the letters 'я', 'ю', 'є', 'ї'
grammar.explanation:
This unit completes the alphabet. The first two units taught 27 letters; this one adds the last six, 'й', 'я', 'ю', 'є', 'ї' and 'ь', for 33 in all, and one mark, the apostrophe. The table lists every letter in alphabetical order with its name, its sound and a word that contains it. Square brackets hold the symbols of the International Phonetic Alphabet, in which each symbol stands for exactly one sound. Three symbols may be new: a raised [ʲ] after a consonant marks it soft (the next note), [ː] marks a long sound, and [ˈ] stands before the stressed syllable.

The letter 'й', named 'йот', writes [j], the 'y' of 'yes'. It is a consonant, so it never makes a syllable by itself. It usually ends a syllable, as in 'чай' [t͡ʃɑj], tea, and in the name 'Андрі́й'.

English writes [j] plus a vowel with two letters, as in 'yes'. Ukrainian usually writes it with one: four vowel letters can include the [j]. They are called iotated vowels, from 'йот':

- 'я' is [jɑ], like 'ya' in 'yard'
- 'ю' is [ju], like 'you'
- 'є' is [jɛ], like 'ye' in 'yes'
- 'ї' is [ji], like 'yea' in 'yeast'

'Я', 'ю' and 'є' have two jobs, and the letter before them decides which one:

- At the start of a word, after a vowel and after the apostrophe (the third note), they are [j] plus a vowel: 'я' [jɑ], I; 'я́блуко' [ˈjɑblukɔ], apple; 'є' [jɛ], there is.
- After a consonant they add no [j]. They make that consonant soft and give the plain vowel [ɑ], [u] or [ɛ]: 'земля́' [zɛmˈlʲɑ], earth; 'ключ' [klʲut͡ʃ], key.

'Ї' has only the first job. It is always [ji] and never softens a consonant, so it is written only at the start of a word, after a vowel or after the apostrophe: 'ї́жа' [ˈjiʒɑ], food; 'Украї́на' [ukrɑˈjinɑ], Ukraine; 'Ки́їв' [ˈkɪjiw], Kyiv. The letter 'і' has no [j]: in 'кіт', cat, the 'і' follows the 'к' directly.

No single letter does for [ɔ] what 'я', 'ю' and 'є' do for the other vowels. [j] plus [ɔ] is written with two letters, 'йо', wherever it is heard: 'йо́га' [ˈjɔɦɑ], yoga. A soft consonant plus [ɔ] is written 'ьо', which the next note explains.

Each of 'я', 'ю', 'є' and 'ї' is one vowel letter and makes one syllable, even when it stands for two sounds: 'я́блуко' has three syllables, я-блу-ко.

rows: between 'v' and 'w'; 'w' in 'cow' at the end of a syllable
a tap or trill of the tongue tip
none; it softens the consonant before it

grammar.title: Hard and soft consonants and the soft sign
grammar.explanation:
Many Ukrainian consonants have two versions, hard and soft. A hard consonant is said much as in English. A soft consonant is said with the middle of the tongue raised toward the hard palate, the hard front part of the roof of the mouth, at the same moment as the consonant itself, as if a light 'y' were blended into it rather than added after it. English comes close in the 'ny' of 'canyon' and the 'll' of 'million'. A raised [ʲ] marks softness: [n] is hard and [nʲ] is soft.

Softness is part of how a word sounds, so it must be heard and said: 'стіл', table, ends in a hard [l], and 'сіль', salt, ends in a soft [lʲ].

These consonants can be hard or soft:

- 'д', 'т', 'з', 'с', 'ц', 'дз'
- 'л', 'н'
- 'р', which can be soft only before a vowel; at the end of a word or before a consonant it is always hard, as in 'ве́чір'

For these consonants, the spelling shows which version you hear through the letter that comes next:

- Before 'і', 'я', 'ю', 'є' and 'ь' the consonant is soft: 'ніс' [nʲis], nose; 'земля́' [zɛmˈlʲɑ], earth; 'день' [dɛnʲ], day.
- Before 'а', 'о', 'у', 'е' and 'и', before another consonant, and at the end of a word with no 'ь', it is hard: 'тут', here; 'сир', cheese; the 'д' of 'день'.

The soft sign 'ь' is named 'м’яки́й знак', literally 'soft sign'. It is a letter with no sound of its own, and its one job is to make the consonant before it soft where no softening vowel letter follows: at the end of a word, as in 'день' [dɛnʲ], day, 'сіль' [sʲilʲ], salt, and 'о́сінь' [ˈɔsʲinʲ], autumn, before another consonant, as in 'Львів' [lʲʋiw], Lviv, and before 'о', as the next paragraph shows. It is written only after the consonants that can be soft, and after 'р' only before 'о'. It never follows 'б', 'п', 'в', 'м', 'ф', 'ж', 'ч', 'ш', 'щ', 'г', 'ґ', 'к' or 'х', because these are never fully soft.

A soft consonant followed by [ɔ] is written with 'ьо': 'сього́дні', today, begins with a soft [sʲ] and then [ɔ]. So 'ьо' does the job that 'я', 'ю' and 'є' do after a consonant, and 'йо' does the job they do at the start of a word or after a vowel.

The other consonants, such as the 'к' of 'кіт' or the 'п' of 'пі́сня', are only slightly softened before 'і', as the first unit noted; they have no separate soft version.

A consonant directly before a soft consonant often turns soft as well. In 'пі́сня', song, the 'с' is soft because the 'н' after it is soft, and in 'сього́дні' the 'д' is soft before the soft 'н'. This happens by itself when you say the soft consonant naturally.

rows: after a consonant that can be soft
after a consonant that can be soft
at the end of a word

grammar.title: The apostrophe and doubled consonants
grammar.explanation:
The apostrophe (’), called 'апостро́ф', is a mark, not a letter, and it has no sound of its own. It stands between a consonant and one of 'я', 'ю', 'є', 'ї', and it tells you two things: the consonant before it stays hard, and the vowel letter after it keeps its [j].

The mark is needed because of the rule of the first note: after a consonant, 'я', 'ю' and 'є' lose their [j] and soften the consonant. The consonants 'б', 'п', 'в', 'м' and 'ф' are never fully soft, so after them the apostrophe shows what to say: 'м’я́со', meat, is [ˈmjɑsɔ], a hard [m], then [j], then [ɑ]. Compare 'земля́' [zɛmˈlʲɑ], where the 'я' after 'л' gives a soft [lʲ] and no [j].

The apostrophe is written in three places:

- after 'б', 'п', 'в', 'м', 'ф' before 'я', 'ю', 'є', 'ї': 'ім’я́' [iˈmjɑ], first name; 'сім’я́' [sʲiˈmjɑ], family; 'м’я́со' [ˈmjɑsɔ], meat
- after 'р' at the end of a syllable, where 'р' is always hard: 'бур’я́н' [buˈrjɑn], weed
- after a prefix that ends in a consonant, before a part that begins with 'я', 'ю', 'є' or 'ї'; a prefix is a part added to the front of a word to change its meaning, as 're-' is in English 'rewrite': 'від’ї́зд' [ʋidˈjizd], departure, is built from the prefix 'від', away from, and a part meaning a journey

The rule stops in two places. In both, no apostrophe is written after 'б', 'п', 'в', 'м' or 'ф', and the consonant is said slightly soft with no separate [j]:

- after another consonant, other than 'р', in the same root, the core part of a word that carries its meaning: 'свя́то' [ˈsʲʋʲɑtɔ], holiday
- before 'я' or 'ю' in some words taken from other languages: 'бюро́' [bʲuˈrɔ], bureau

A doubled consonant letter stands for one long consonant, held about twice as long as a single one, not for two separate sounds. English has long consonants mainly where two words meet, as in 'black cat' or 'ten nights'. In 'життя́' [ʒɪˈtʲːɑ], life, the 'тт' is one long soft [tʲː], soft because 'я' follows; in 'знання́' [znɑˈnʲːɑ], knowledge, the 'нн' is one long soft [nʲː]. A doubled consonant can also be hard: the woman's name 'Га́нна' [ˈɦɑnːɑ] has a long hard [nː]. Hold the consonant; do not say it twice.

rows: hard consonant, then [j] and the vowel
after a prefix ending in a consonant
before 'я' or 'ю' in some borrowed words

grammar.title: A procedure for reading any new word
grammar.explanation:
Ukrainian spelling follows pronunciation closely: each letter stands for one sound or a small set of sounds, and the letters around it decide which. With the whole alphabet learned, you can read any word aloud by looking at it in a fixed order:

- Step 1: find the apostrophe. The consonant before it is hard, and the vowel letter after it begins with [j].
- Step 2: look at each 'я', 'ю' and 'є'. At the start of a word, after a vowel or after the apostrophe it is [j] plus a vowel; after a consonant it softens that consonant and is a plain vowel. 'Ї' is always [ji].
- Step 3: look at the letter after each other consonant. A consonant that can be soft is soft before 'і' or 'ь', also in 'ьо', and hard before 'а', 'о', 'у', 'е', 'и' or another consonant and at the end of the word, except that it often turns soft before a soft consonant. The other consonants are only slightly softened before 'і'. The 'ь' itself is not said.
- Step 4: join the letters that make one sound: 'дж' and 'дз' within a root, and any doubled letter, which is one long consonant. Read 'щ' as [ʃt͡ʃ].
- Step 5: check each 'в' and the end of the word. 'В' is [ʋ] before a vowel and [w] at the end of a syllable, and voiced consonants such as 'б', 'д' and 'з' stay voiced at the end of a word.
- Step 6: find the stress mark and say that syllable louder and longer. The next unit explains stress.
- Step 7: say the word slowly, syllable by syllable, then at normal speed.

Here are five worked examples:

- 'Украї́на': there is no apostrophe; the 'ї' after the vowel 'а' is [ji]; the 'к' and the 'р' stand before a consonant and before 'а', so both are hard; the stress is on 'ї': [ukrɑˈjinɑ].
- 'сім’я́': the apostrophe keeps the 'м' hard and makes the 'я' [jɑ]; the 'с' is soft before 'і'; the stress is on 'я': [sʲiˈmjɑ].
- 'життя́': the 'ж' is [ʒ] and the 'и' is [ɪ]; 'тт' is one long consonant, soft before 'я'; the stress is on 'я': [ʒɪˈtʲːɑ].
- 'сього́дні': 'сьо' is a soft [sʲ] and then [ɔ]; the 'г' is [ɦ]; the 'н' is soft before 'і', and the 'д' before it softens too; the stress is on the second 'о': [sʲɔˈɦɔdʲnʲi].
- 'Львів': 'ль' is a soft [lʲ] with no vowel; the 'в' before 'і' is [ʋ]; the final 'в' is [w]; with one syllable there is no stress mark: [lʲʋiw].

rows: Hard consonant before it; [j] after it
[j] plus a vowel, or a soft consonant plus a vowel; 'ї' is always [ji]
Soft before 'і', 'ь', 'ьо', and often before a soft consonant; hard elsewhere
One sound each; a doubled letter is one long consonant
Each 'в' and the end of the word
Say that syllable louder and longer
Say it slowly by syllables, then at speed

culture.title: Letters as symbols, and a day for the written language
culture.text:
The Ukrainian alphabet has 33 letters, and Ukrainians are attached to several of them. The letter 'ї' has become a popular symbol of the language: it appears on its own on posters, badges and T-shirts and in street art, because it is so typical of Ukrainian spelling. The apostrophe matters too: it is part of the correct spelling of everyday words such as 'ім’я́' and 'сім’я́'.

The letter 'ґ' has its own history. It was removed from official spelling in 1933 and restored in 1990, and words such as 'ґа́нок', porch, are written with it again. The current rules of spelling were adopted in 2019, and this course follows them.

Every year on November 9, Ukraine marks the Day of Ukrainian Writing and Language. The day was set in 1997 on what was then the church feast day of Nestor the Chronicler, a monk of Kyiv who is traditionally named as the author of one of the oldest chronicles of the region. Since 2000 the national radio has broadcast a dictation on that day: a text is read aloud slowly, and people across the country and abroad, from schoolchildren to well-known public figures, write it down and then check their spelling. The dictation exercises in this unit work the same way.

When Ukrainians spell a word aloud, on the phone or at a counter, they name its letters as Oksana does in this unit's first dialogue. Three of these names are words of their own rather than a sound plus a vowel:

- 'йот' for 'й'
- 'м’яки́й знак' for 'ь'
- 'апостро́ф' for the apostrophe

exercises.prompt: How many letters does the Ukrainian alphabet have?
exercises.explanation: This unit adds 'й', 'я', 'ю', 'є', 'ї' and 'ь' to the 27 letters of the first two units. The apostrophe is a mark, not a letter.

exercises.prompt: Match each letter name with its letter
exercises.explanation: 'М’яки́й знак' is literally 'soft sign', and 'йот' is a name of its own. The other names are a vowel plus the sound of the letter, or the sound plus a vowel.

exercises.prompt: Which sound does 'й' write, as at the end of 'чай'?
choices: No sound; it softens the consonant before it
exercises.explanation: 'Й', named 'йот', is the consonant [j]. 'Чай' is said [t͡ʃɑj], in one syllable.
'Ключ' is [klʲut͡ʃ], with a soft 'л' before 'ю'. Tea is 'чай' and a cat is 'кіт'.

exercises.prompt: How is 'я' said at the start of a word, as in 'я́блуко'?
exercises.explanation: At the start of a word, after a vowel and after the apostrophe, 'я' is [j] plus [ɑ].
The word for 'I' is the letter 'я', written small inside a sentence. Ukrainian needs no word for 'am'.
The soft sign has no sound. It makes the consonant before it soft: 'день' is [dɛnʲ].

exercises.prompt: Where can the letter 'ї' be written?
choices: Directly after any consonant, which it softens
Only at the start of a word, after a vowel or after the apostrophe
Only at the end of a word
exercises.explanation: 'Ї' is always [ji] and never softens a consonant, so it never follows one directly: 'ї́жа', 'Украї́на', 'Ки́їв'.
'М’я́со' is [ˈmjɑsɔ]: a hard [m], then [jɑ]. Fish is 'ри́ба' and cheese is 'сир'.
'Є' says that something exists or is present. It is said [jɛ], because it stands at the start of a word.

exercises.prompt_source: Spell 'Ки́їв' aloud: К, И, Ї, В.
exercises.explanation: The second letter is 'и', named 'и'; the third is 'ї', named 'ї'. The letter 'і' does not appear in this word.

exercises.prompt: What does 'я' do after the 'л' of 'земля́'?
choices: It makes the 'л' soft and gives a plain [ɑ].
exercises.explanation: After a consonant, 'я' loses its [j] and softens the consonant: [zɛmˈlʲɑ].

exercises.prompt: Which of these words ends in a soft consonant?
exercises.explanation: The soft sign at the end of 'сіль' makes the 'л' soft. 'Стіл', 'ніс' and 'сир' end in a consonant with no 'ь', so it is hard.
'Сіль' ends in a soft [lʲ], 'стіл' in a hard [l], and 'сир' in [r].

exercises.hint_source: Here it is winter, and there it is autumn.
exercises.explanation: The word for autumn ends in 'нь': the soft sign makes the 'н' soft. The 'с' is soft before 'і'.

exercises.prompt: Which group of letters is never followed by 'ь'?
exercises.explanation: The soft sign follows only consonants that can be soft. 'Б', 'п', 'в', 'м', 'ф', 'ж', 'ч', 'ш', 'щ', 'г', 'ґ', 'к' and 'х' are never fully soft.
'Ключ' has a soft 'л' before 'ю'. Ukrainian needs no word for 'is' here.

exercises.prompt: Match the Ukrainian with the English
exercises.explanation: Three of these words have the apostrophe, which keeps the consonant before 'я' hard and the [j] sounded.

exercises.prompt: Why is there an apostrophe in 'м’я́со'?
choices: It keeps the 'м' hard and shows that [j] is said before the vowel.
It shows that a letter has been left out.
exercises.explanation: After 'б', 'п', 'в', 'м', 'ф' the apostrophe keeps the consonant hard and the [j] of 'я' sounded: [ˈmjɑsɔ].

exercises.prompt_target: Це ___: ма́ма, та́то, брат і сестра́.
exercises.hint_source: This is a family: mom, dad, brother and sister.
exercises.explanation: The word for family is [sʲiˈmjɑ]: a hard 'м' followed by [jɑ], so it is written with the apostrophe.

exercises.prompt_source: Spell 'Львів' aloud: Л, soft sign, В, І, В.
exercises.explanation: The soft sign comes right after 'л' and is named with two words, 'м’яки́й знак'.

choices: Two [t] sounds said one after the other
A hard [t] followed by a soft [tʲ]
One long soft consonant, held longer than a single one
exercises.explanation: A doubled consonant letter is one long consonant. Here it is soft because 'я' follows: [ʒɪˈtʲːɑ].
The word for life is written with a doubled 'тт', one long soft consonant, and ends in 'я'.

exercises.prompt: What does 'сьо' write at the start of 'сього́дні'?
exercises.explanation: After a consonant, 'ьо' writes a soft consonant plus [ɔ]. 'Йо' writes [jɔ] at the start of a word or after a vowel.

choices: There it is day, and here it is evening.
Here it is day, and there it is evening.
There it is autumn, and here it is winter.
exercises.explanation: The sentence begins with 'там', there, and 'день' ends in a soft 'н'.
Write the apostrophe after 'м': the 'м' is hard and the 'я' keeps its [j].

exercises.hint_source: The bread and salt are here.
exercises.explanation: The word for salt is [sʲilʲ]: a soft 'с' before 'і' and a soft 'л', which needs the soft sign.

exercises.prompt_source: The tea is here, and the coffee is there.
exercises.explanation: 'А' joins two contrasting statements. 'Чи' means 'or' and does not belong here.

exercises.hint_source: I am here, and the family is there.
exercises.explanation: 'Я' is written small only inside a sentence; here it starts the sentence. 'Сім’я́' has the apostrophe after 'м'.
The 'с' is soft before 'і'. The apostrophe keeps the 'м' hard: [sʲiˈmjɑ].

exercises.prompt: Read 'пі́сня' by the procedure. Which consonant is soft only because a soft consonant follows it?
exercises.explanation: By step 3, a consonant that can be soft often turns soft before a soft consonant. The 'н' is soft because 'я' follows it, and the 'с' before it softens too. The 'п' has no soft version.
'Ки́їв' has 'и' and then 'ї', which is [ji] after a vowel. 'Львів' has the soft sign after 'л'.

exercises.prompt_source: Today there is cheese and bread.
exercises.explanation: 'Є' follows 'сього́дні' and comes before the things named, in the same order as the English.

exercises.hint_source: There is tea and an apple here.
exercises.explanation: 'Чай' ends in 'й'. 'Я́блуко' starts with 'я', which is [jɑ] at the start of a word.
